The excrements of the first and second <term>coctions</term> <gloss>digestions</gloss> (namely in the intestines, and the bladders of urine and gall) are contemporary with the digesting organs themselves. Finally, not only in the vegetative part of the soul, but even before the soul itself, there exists mind, providence, and intellect; which from the very first origin, dispose, ordain, and procure all things for the being and well-being of the chick; and through art, they fashion it into the form and likeness of the parents.

Regarding this likeness of the offspring, one may doubt what the cause is why sometimes the fetus is found more like the father, sometimes the mother, and sometimes even like ancestors, whether paternal or maternal? Especially since many eggs are fecundated by a single mating at the same moment. It is also wonderful that virtues and vices, diseases also, marks, and moles, are transferred from the parents to the descendants; and that into only some of the fetuses, but not into all. In the race of poultry, some are noble and born for battle; who prefer to die rather than yield to adversaries by fleeing: yet their descendants, unless they were born from similar parents, gradually cast off that virtue; according to that saying: the brave are created by the brave. In most other species of animals also (and especially in humans) nobility of race is observed; and many endowments of mind and body come to them by descent.

I have often wondered at this: why, when we see the offspring (for the most part) obtain a certain mixed fabric or composition from both parents, and that in all other parts; yet the same does not happen in the genitals: but for the most part either a male or a female is born, and very rarely indeed a hermaphrodite?

Finally, many things are present before they appear; and certain things are begun among the first which are finished last; such as the eyes, the genitals, and the beak.

From this also arise certain doubts and difficulties concerning the primacy of the limbs or the dignity of the parts;

<summary>Harvey explores the inheritance of physical and behavioral traits from parents to offspring and questions why sexual characteristics usually remain distinct rather than mixed.</summary>
